content: Nonmetals are a classification of chemical elements based on their general physical and chemical properties. In the periodic table, elements are broadly categorized as either metals or nonmetals, with a few elements exhibiting intermediate properties referred to as metalloids. The elements commonly recognized as nonmetals include hydrogen (H), carbon (C) from Group 14, nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) from Group 15 (the pnictogens), oxygen (O), sulfur (S), and selenium (Se) from Group 16 (the chalcogens), all elements in Group 17 (the halogens), and all elements in Group 18 (the noble gases). There is no strict definition for the term nonmetal, as it encompasses a range of behaviors. However, nonmetals generally exhibit the following characteristics: They are poor conductors of heat and electricity compared to metals. They form acidic oxides, in contrast to metals, which typically form basic oxides. In their solid state, nonmetals are dull and brittle, unlike metals, which are lustrous, ductile, and malleable. Nonmetals usually have lower densities than metals. Their melting points and boiling points are significantly lower than those of metals. Nonmetals have high electronegativity. They typically lack luster or shine. Only 18 elements in the periodic table are generally considered nonmetals, compared to over 80 metals. Despite their smaller number, nonmetals constitute the majority of the Earth's crust, atmosphere, and oceans. Furthermore, the bulk tissues of living organisms are composed almost entirely of nonmetals. Many nonmetals, such as hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine, exist as diatomic molecules, while most of the remaining nonmetals are polyatomic in nature. Interestingly, even these 20 nonmetallic elements tend to exhibit metallic properties when subjected to extremely high pressures, such as those around 300 GPa.
